title: Why Are the Biggest AI Data Centers Built in the Desert?

beats.say: Servers hate heat. Like, really hate it.
So why are companies building some of the biggest ones in the hottest, driest places on Earth?
Arizona. Nevada. Abu Dhabi.
It sounds like the worst idea ever. But there's a genuinely smart reason behind it. And a pretty big catch.
Let's get into it.

parts.chapter: PART 1: WHAT IS A DATA CENTER?

beats.say: First, what even is a data center? It's a giant building packed with computers called servers, stacked in rows and running twenty-four seven.

visual.label: DATA CENTER = A BUILDING FULL OF SERVERS

beats.say: Every video you stream, every photo you back up, every question you ask an AI, it gets handled in a place like this.
And here's the thing. All those computers turn electricity into heat. A lot of heat.
Engineers try to keep the air going into servers between about eighteen and twenty-seven degrees Celsius. Too hot, and things slow down or break.

Now add AI. The International Energy Agency expects data centers worldwide to more than double their electricity use by 2030, to around nine hundred forty-five terawatt-hours. That's slightly more than the whole of Japan uses today.

visual.bottom: ≈ MORE THAN ALL OF JAPAN USES TODAY

beats.say: So companies need more data centers, fast. And they need a lot of room to put them.

parts.chapter: PART 2: DRY AIR IS A CHEAT CODE

beats.say: So why the desert? Reason number one sounds completely backwards. Dry air.
Ever felt cold getting out of a pool, even on a warm day? That's evaporation. When water evaporates, it carries heat away with it.

visual.label: EVAPORATION = HEAT LEAVING WITH THE WATER

beats.say: Lots of data centers use that same trick. Fans pull hot air through wet pads, the water evaporates, and the air comes out cooler.
And here's the key. It works best when the air is dry. In humid places, the air is already full of moisture, so water evaporates more slowly and the trick works way worse.
The US Department of Energy says this kind of cooling can drop air temperature by fifteen to forty degrees Fahrenheit, using about a quarter of the energy of central air conditioning.
There's a bonus, too. Humidity is bad news for electronics. Too much moisture can cause corrosion that damages circuit boards.
So yes, the desert is hot. But it's dry hot. And for cooling computers, dry beats humid.
Quick thing. I'm a new creator, and if you're learning something, hitting subscribe genuinely helps me make more of these. Okay, back to the desert.

parts.chapter: PART 3: LAND, POWER, SUN AND TAXES

beats.say: Reason two: space. Deserts have huge stretches of flat, empty land, and it's usually cheap. Data centers are enormous, so that matters.

Take the Switch Citadel campus near Reno, Nevada. It sits on about two thousand acres, right next to Tesla's Gigafactory. It's designed for up to seven point two million square feet of data center space and up to six hundred fifty megawatts of power. When it opened in 2017, Switch called it the largest data center campus in the world.
Reason three: power and sunshine. Data centers need huge amounts of reliable electricity, and deserts get tons of sun for solar. Switch says its campus runs on one hundred percent renewable energy.

Reason four: money and location. In 2021, Arizona extended tax breaks on data center equipment all the way to 2033. And the Southwest is home to nearly a fifth of all Americans, so data doesn't have to travel far to reach them.

And it's not just the US. In Abu Dhabi, a group including OpenAI, Oracle and Nvidia is building Stargate UAE, a one-gigawatt AI cluster inside a five-gigawatt AI campus. The first two hundred megawatts are planned for 2026.
Real question for you. Would you want a giant data center in your neighborhood? Yes or no, tell me in the comments.
But here's the catch. Remember that evaporation trick? It uses water. And deserts don't exactly have a lot of that.

Arizona has more than a hundred and fifty data centers. Independent estimates say a single data center can use anywhere from fifty thousand to five million gallons of water a day, depending on how it's cooled.

visual.bottom: EACH: ~50,000 TO 5,000,000 GALLONS OF WATER A DAY

beats.say: The sustainability group Ceres estimates data centers in the Phoenix area used about three hundred eighty-five million gallons a year. In a worst case, that could grow about ten times. And the power plants feeding them could use even more water.

visual.title: PHOENIX-AREA DATA CENTERS, WATER PER YEAR

beats.say: Now, plot twist. Farming uses more than seventy percent of Arizona's water. Even that worst case for data centers is about one percent of the Phoenix area's home water use. So data centers aren't the biggest water user. They're just one of the fastest growing.

visual.label: OF ARIZONA'S WATER GOES TO FARMING
visual.note: DATA CENTERS, WORST CASE ≈ 1% OF PHOENIX HOME USE

beats.say: And companies are reacting. Microsoft says its water-cooled Arizona data centers only use up water when it's hotter than about eighty-five degrees Fahrenheit, and it'll build only zero-water data centers in Arizona from now on. Google said its Mesa site won't use evaporative coolers at all.

Some cities are pushing back too. In August 2025, Tucson's city council voted unanimously against bringing a giant data center project called Project Blue into the city, after weeks of residents worrying about water, electricity bills and secrecy.
If that vote surprised you, hit like. It helps more people find these videos.
So, genius or problem? Honestly, both.
The desert gives data centers dry air for cheap cooling, tons of space, sunshine and tax breaks. But it also puts thirsty, power-hungry machines in places where water is precious.

left: DRY AIR · SPACE · SUN · TAX BREAKS

beats.say: And with AI pushing data center electricity use to more than double by 2030, these fights are only getting bigger. The next wave is moving to closed-loop cooling that reuses the same water, or no water at all.
So here's my question. If you were in charge, where would you build the next giant AI data center? The desert, somewhere freezing cold, or space? Drop it in the comments.

description: Servers hate heat, so why are some of the biggest data centers being built in the desert? Bojji breaks down the dry-air cooling trick, cheap land, power, sun and tax breaks, and the big catch: water.
sources: US Department of Energy, Evaporative Coolers
